name: Network Address Translation
statement: Let many devices share one public IP address by rewriting addresses in packets as they pass a router.
statementAccent: share one public IP address by rewriting addresses
meaning: Network Address Translation, or NAT, is a method of mapping one IP address space into another by modifying network address information in the IP header of packets while they are in transit across a routing device, such as a home or office router. The most common form maps multiple private IP addresses, used inside a local network, for instance in the 192.168 range, to a single public IP address used on the Internet, so that many devices on a home or office network share one public address; this is the near-universal setup for home routers. A major reason NAT became widespread is to conserve IPv4 addresses and mitigate their exhaustion: instead of every device needing its own scarce public IPv4 address, a whole network can hide behind one. The common variant is Port Address Translation, also called NAT overload or masquerading, in which the router keeps a translation table tracking connections and uses port numbers to distinguish which internal device each connection belongs to, so that return traffic is routed back to the correct internal host; it rewrites the source address and port on outgoing packets and the destination address and port on returning packets. NAT has side effects. It provides a degree of incidental security or isolation, because internal hosts are not directly addressable from outside, but it also breaks end-to-end connectivity and complicates protocols and peer-to-peer applications, requiring workarounds such as port forwarding and hole punching. NAT has been hugely important in extending the life of IPv4 and is ubiquitous in home and enterprise networks, while IPv6's vast address space reduces the need for it.
mechanism: Network Address Translation works by having a router rewrite the addressing information inside packets as they cross the boundary between a private network and the public Internet, so that an entire internal network can present itself to the outside world through a single public address. Inside the local network, devices use private IP addresses, drawn from ranges reserved for internal use and not routable on the public Internet. When an internal device sends a packet out, the NAT router intercepts it and changes the packet's source address from the device's private address to the router's own public address, so that to the outside world the traffic appears to come from the router. The challenge is the return trip: many internal devices may be communicating through the same public address at once, so when a reply comes back, the router must know which internal device it belongs to. Port Address Translation solves this by using port numbers. As each outgoing connection passes through, the router records, in a translation table, the mapping between the internal device's private address and port and a port on the public side, and it rewrites the packet accordingly; when a reply arrives addressed to that public port, the router looks up the table, restores the original private address and port as the destination, and forwards the packet to the correct internal device. In this way a single public address, multiplexed across thousands of port numbers, can serve a whole network. This mechanism has a natural consequence: because external hosts cannot initiate connections to internal devices that have no table entry, internal machines are hidden, giving incidental protection, but it also means the clean end-to-end model of the Internet, in which any host can directly address any other, is broken, complicating peer-to-peer and server applications and requiring techniques like port forwarding and hole punching to reach inside.

examples.text: A home router maps many private addresses like 192.168 addresses to its single public IP address.
Port Address Translation uses a table of port numbers to route each reply back to the right internal device.
A whole network hides behind one public address, easing IPv4 address exhaustion.

variants.name: Port Address Translation
variants.text: The common overload form using port numbers so many devices share one public address, also called masquerading.

variants.name: Breaking end-to-end
variants.text: NAT gives incidental isolation but complicates peer-to-peer and inbound connections, needing port forwarding or hole punching.

whyItMatters: Network Address Translation is one of the technologies that quietly kept the Internet running as it outgrew its own addressing, and it is present in virtually every home and office network in the world. Its central importance is conservation: the IPv4 address space, with about 4.3 billion addresses, proved far too small for a world of billions of devices, and NAT dramatically stretched it by letting entire networks share a single public address, hiding dozens or thousands of internal devices behind one. Without NAT, the IPv4 Internet would have run out of addresses long before IPv6 could be deployed, so NAT bought the crucial time that kept the Internet growing. Beyond conservation, NAT reshaped the practical architecture of networking: the near-universal home router that connects a household's devices to the Internet works by performing NAT, and the private-address-behind-a-public-address pattern is now the default way most devices connect. NAT also provides a measure of incidental security, since machines behind it are not directly reachable from outside. Yet it is a consequential compromise, breaking the Internet's original end-to-end principle and complicating peer-to-peer applications, a tension that partly motivates the move to IPv6 and its restoration of unique addresses. As the technique that lets many devices share one public IP address by rewriting packet headers, NAT has been essential to the Internet's survival and shape.

working.text: change a packet's private source address to the router's public address as it leaves the network.
record the mapping in a translation table keyed by port so replies can be matched to the right device.
look up returning packets in the table and rewrite the destination to the correct internal address and port.

limits: NAT is enormously useful but it is a compromise with real drawbacks that reward care. Its most significant cost is breaking the Internet's end-to-end connectivity: because internal devices are not directly addressable from outside, external hosts cannot initiate connections to them without special arrangements, which complicates servers, peer-to-peer applications, voice and video calling, and online gaming, and forces workarounds like port forwarding, STUN, and hole punching. The incidental security NAT provides, by hiding internal hosts, is a side effect and not a substitute for a real firewall, and treating NAT as a security mechanism is a mistake. NAT also adds state and processing to the router, which must maintain the translation table, and it can interfere with protocols that embed addresses in their data. NAT is fundamentally a workaround for IPv4 address scarcity; IPv6's vast address space removes the need for it and restores unique addressing, though NAT persists widely. Some technical details reward care: NAT modifies the IP header in transit; the common port-based form is formally called NAPT, with PAT, NAT overload, and masquerading as synonyms; and it maps many private addresses to one public address. So NAT robustly lets networks share a public address and conserve IPv4, understood as a workaround that breaks end-to-end connectivity and provides only incidental, not real, security.
misreadings: NAT is not a firewall; its hiding of internal hosts is incidental, not real security. It does not preserve the Internet's end-to-end model, complicating inbound and peer-to-peer connections. And it is a workaround for IPv4 scarcity, not a permanent design, so treating NAT as a security solution, as transparent to all applications, or as a feature rather than a stopgap, misreads it.
origin: The technique of rewriting IP addresses in packet headers at a router so that many private devices share one public IP address, developed to conserve scarce IPv4 addresses.
